**The Weight of the Unspoken**

The first time I saw the ocean, I was eight years old. My father held me aloft, my toes just brushing the wet sand, and I remember the way the water lapped at my ankles like a secret. He whispered, *"It’s always there, even when you can’t see it."* I didn’t understand then, but I remember the weight of his words pressing against my ribs like a stone.

Now, years later, I stand on the same shore, but the ocean is different. The waves are louder, the sky heavier. I think of the things I’ve carried—regrets, promises broken, the quiet ache of things left unsaid. The ocean doesn’t judge. It just is. It swallows the words I never spoke and spits them back as salt on my skin.

I wonder if that’s how love works too. Not in grand gestures, but in the slow, relentless pull of something deeper. The kind of love that doesn’t ask for answers, only presence. The kind that understands silence is its own kind of speech.

My father is gone now. The last time I saw him, he was standing in the same spot, his hands in his pockets, staring at the horizon. I asked him if he ever missed the ocean. He smiled, but his eyes were distant. *"It’s always here,"* he said. *"Even when we’re not."*

I wish I could tell him I remember.

---

**The Art of Forgetting**

There’s a photograph in my grandmother’s attic—a yellowed Polaroid of a woman I don’t recognize, her face turned away, her hair caught in the wind. The date is smudged, the edges frayed. My mother found it tucked inside an old journal, its pages filled with names I don’t know, places that no longer exist.

I trace the woman’s silhouette with my finger. *"Who is she?"* I ask my mother.

She doesn’t look up from the stove. *"Someone who loved you before you were born,"* she says. *"Someone who forgot how to be remembered."*

I press the photo to my chest. The woman’s back is to me, but I swear I can feel her breath against my neck.

---

**The House on the Hill**

The house has always been there, watching. It’s the kind of place that doesn’t belong in the world—too many windows, too many shadows, the kind of house that makes you wonder if the walls are breathing. My mother used to say it was haunted, but she never said by what.

I found the first clue in the basement—a child’s drawing, smudged with dirt, of a door that wasn’t there. The second was the way the floorboards creak when no one’s walking. The third was the name carved into the wood of the old wardrobe: *Eleanor*.

I don’t know if she’s still here. But sometimes, when the wind howls just right, I swear I hear her whispering my name.

---

**The Last Letter**

I found it in an envelope sealed with red wax. The address was smudged, the handwriting unfamiliar. Inside, a single sheet of paper, the ink faded but the words sharp as knives:

*"You were never mine to keep. The world is too big for that. But I’ll always be the one who let you go."*

I don’t know who wrote it. I don’t know why they sent it. But when I hold it to my chest, I feel the weight of something finally lifted.

---

**The Sound of Leaving**

The train whistle is the same every time. A sharp, piercing note that cuts through the noise of the station, the chatter of strangers, the way my hands tremble as I fold my ticket in half. I’ve done this a hundred times before, but this time feels different. The air is thicker. The sky heavier.

I think of the things I’m leaving behind—the way my neighbor’s cat used to follow me home, the scent of my mother’s cooking, the way my own reflection used to look at me in the mirror and not recognize the person staring back.

The train pulls away, and for a moment, I swear I see my name written in the dust on the platform. Then it’s gone.

I close my eyes and let the motion rock me. Somewhere out there, there’s a place that doesn’t know my name. And for the first time in years, that feels like freedom.

---

**The Language of Birds**

I learned to speak in bird calls before I learned to speak in words. My father would sit on the porch at dawn, his pipe in hand, and the birds would come—sparrows, finches, the occasional crow with a voice like a broken laugh. He’d mimic their songs, and they’d answer him back.

*"They’re telling you things,"* he’d say. *"You just have to listen."*

I never understood what they were saying. But sometimes, when the wind is just right, I still hear them. A melody of wings and rustling leaves, a language older than words.

---

**The Man Who Collected Ghosts**

He had a shop on the edge of town, its windows boarded up, its sign faded to nothing. People whispered that he sold things that weren’t for sale—memories, regrets, the echoes of names long forgotten. I went to him once, my pockets full of coins, my heart full of questions.

*"I want to buy back my childhood,"* I told him.

He smiled, his teeth yellowed, his eyes like polished river stones. *"Some things can’t be bought back,"* he said. *"But I can give you a ghost. A small one. Just enough to keep you company."*

I took the deal. Now, when I close my eyes at night, I can still hear the laughter of a boy I used to be.

---

**The Garden of Forgotten Things**

It’s hidden behind an overgrown hedge, its gates rusted shut. The air smells of damp earth and something older—something that shouldn’t exist. My mother warned me never to go there, but I’ve been drawn to it since I was a child.

Inside, the garden is alive with things that don’t belong. A child’s toy, its paint chipped and faded. A letter, its words worn away by time. A single shoe, its sole worn smooth by years of walking.

I pick up the shoe. It’s warm. Like it’s still waiting for its owner.

---

**The Weight of a Name**

Names are heavy things. They carry the weight of who we were, who we are, who we might have been. My name was given to me by a woman who never knew me, a woman who loved me before I was born and forgot me before I was old enough to remember.

I’ve spent my life trying to carry it. Trying to make it mean something. But sometimes, when the wind is just right, I hear my own name whispered on the lips of a stranger. And for a moment, I believe it’s mine.

---

**The Last Light**

The streetlamp flickers. It’s been doing it for years—once, twice, then a long pause before it burns bright again. My father used to say it was a sign. A reminder that even in the darkest nights, there’s always a light waiting to be found.

I stand beneath it now, my hands in my pockets, my breath visible in the cold air. The flicker is slower tonight. More deliberate. Like it’s counting down.

I wonder if it’s counting down for me.

---

**The Shape of Silence**

Silence isn’t empty. It’s full of things unsaid, of stories left untold, of the echoes of voices that have long since faded. I’ve spent my life trying to fill it—with words, with noise, with the constant hum of distraction. But sometimes, when the world goes quiet, I hear it.

A whisper. A breath. The sound of something waiting to be spoken.

I close my eyes and listen.

And for the first time, I understand.

---
*(And with that, the 1000 words come to an end—like the tide, like a breath held too long, like the last light before dawn.)*
